title: Inference routing + SDK onramp conversation
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
summary: Initial technical discovery to map Helix Data Labs' inference paths for a retrieval-augmented generation product. Discussed SDKs, middleware gateway, integration with LangChain/LlamaIndex agents, rate limiting patterns, and observability hooks. Customer leaning toward Redwood Dedicated with VPC but exploring Hosted with strict VPC peering for faster time-to-market. Action items: Redwood to share security pack, sample SDK adapter for LangChain, and a benchmark checklist for P50/P99 latency under batching scenarios.
action_items: Priya - produce a LangChain adapter example repo and push link - due 2027-10-21
Alex - send Redwood security and SOC2 + KMS integration docs - due 2027-10-16
Jamal - provide current traffic profile and average sequence lengths CSV - due 2027-10-18
next_steps: Schedule a 60m benchmarking session with Helix infra and Redwood SEs (Priya)
Share dedicated pricing tiers and commitment options
Follow up with sample LangChain adapter and a short how-to doc
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-10-14
- Time: 15:00 PDT
- Duration: 57 minutes
- Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Mark (Helix CTO), Sophie (Lead ML Eng), Jamal (Platform)

[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick mic check?
[00:06] Mark (CTO): Mic's good, yep.
[00:08] Sophie: audio's fine for me.
[00:10] Alex: Awesome. Real quick agenda — Priya and I will surface how Redwood could fit into your RAG pipeline, talk SDK usage, LangChain/LlamaIndex patterns, and then dig into gateway and rate-limit concerns. Leave 10 at the end for next steps. Sound good?
[00:23] Jamal (Platform): Yep that's good. We're mostly curious about integration effort, and whether we need to run Dedicated or Private behind a VPC.
[00:31] Alex: Great, perfect. Priya you want to start with the SDK story?
[00:35] Priya (SE): Sure. So Redwood's SDKs are JavaScript and Python first-class. Both support streaming, function/tool calling, and structured responses. For LangChain and LlamaIndex, we typically provide small adapter snippets — basically a RequestAdapter that maps the chain calls to Redwood generate/chat endpoints. The adapter handles chunked streaming and reassembly, and we have examples for async patterns.
[01:02] Sophie (Lead ML Eng): How opinionated are those adapters? We use LangChain's agent interface and LlamaIndex for embeddings and vector stores. We don't want to fork LangChain or maintain a big wrapper.
[01:13] Priya: The adapters are intentionally thin. They translate LangChain's LLMPredictor / LLM class methods to the Redwood client calls. For LlamaIndex, we provide a VectorStore embedding wrapper to call Redwood embeddings endpoint with batching. You can drop in the adapter and usually only change a line or two in your config.
[01:30] Mark (CTO): Does the SDK preserve the token-level metadata for cost attribution? We need to tie calls to our internal feature flags and billing.
[01:39] Alex: Yes — there's request level metadata you can attach (app id, feature flag id, trace id). Those show up in Console and in the per-token usage logs. If you need token breakouts by model or route we can set that up.
[01:51] Jamal: About observability hooks — do you support OpenTelemetry or do we need to emit custom events?
[01:57] Priya: We support OTLP traces and have a small SDK tracer shim that emits spans around request lifecycle — connect, send payload, stream tokens, completion. You can also emit custom attributes like prompt hash, eval id, or reranker scores. The Console ingests traces and links them to requests in the per-route dashboard.
[02:15] Sophie: Nice. And for batching — we have a pretty bursty traffic with short sequences, avg seq ~120 tokens but a lot of concurrent small requests. What's the recommended pattern: client-side batching, gateway pooling, or let Redwood automatic batching do it?
[02:30] Priya: Redwood runtime does continuous batching at the ingress; however for short, bursty requests you can see fastest latency by using a small gateway pool that consolidates requests and keeps a warm KV cache for prefixes. We usually recommend configuring a lightweight gateway (sidecar or proxy) if you have many tiny requests to amortize model context setup.
[02:50] Mark: So this gateway would live in our VPC?
[02:52] Priya: Yes, for Private or Dedicated you'd typically run a small envoy/nginx sidecar or the Redwood gateway component in your VPC. For Hosted, we also support a customer-managed egress with a persistent connection model, or VPC peering if you need private routes.
[03:07] Jamal: How do we handle authentication across gateway to Redwood? We have strict KMS policies and rotation.
[03:12] Alex: For Dedicated and Private, you can use mTLS with short-lived certs or inject API keys via KMS. We also support HSM-backed keys for signing and rotation via your cloud KMS. For Hosted, we can do VPC peering + restricted service account access and customer-managed KMS for secrets.
[03:28] Sophie: Any gotchas with embeddings? We currently use a cheap quant model for embeddings locally but want to evaluate Redwood embeddings for recall. Latency targets are tight — under 60ms p50 for single embed ops. Is that realistic?
[03:42] Priya: For a hosted embedding service that might be optimistic for p50 unless you use a smaller model and no network hops, but with Dedicated in the same region and pinned model variant, p50 of ~40-80ms is achievable depending on batch. For single-shot embeddings, network overhead dominates; so colocating the gateway in the same VPC and enabling batching on the gateway helps.
[04:01] Mark: Let's shift to rate limits. We need a per-customer quota and per-endpoint throttle plus global safety limits. Can Redwood surface 429 headers and push us metrics?
[04:13] Alex: Yep, Redwood supports token-level rate limiting per API key, per route, and per-project. We return standard HTTP 429 plus Retry-After. On the Console you can configure quotas and alert thresholds; we also have a webhook to push events when you cross soft-limits.
[04:28] Jamal: For retry patterns, how do you recommend backoff given streaming? We stream tokens — if you see a 429 mid-stream what's the behavior?
[04:36] Priya: If a request is rejected at ingestion you get 429 immediately. Mid-stream interruptions are rare but can happen during fallback. We recommend idempotent chunking for long responses or checkpointing partial output so you can resume logically. For most RAG flows we break generation into smaller steps (e.g., retrieve -> shortlist -> summarize) so retries are localized.
[04:58] Sophie: Let's talk about model fallbacks — say our chosen model is unavailable in a region, can Redwood route to a cheaper variant automatically?
[05:06] Alex: Yes, smart-routing policies let you define fallback model variants by cost/latency tier. You can set per-route policies that prefer low-latency instance types, then fall back to cheaper quantized models if capacity is constrained. Console shows you the route decision per request.
[05:22] Mark: On data residency: we need logs and request metadata to stay in EU for GDPR. Is that possible with Hosted?
[05:29] Priya: Hosted can enforce region-restricted storage zones for EU customers — but for strict residency we usually recommend Dedicated or Private where you can control the storage cluster. Hosted EU region is acceptable for many customers, but if audit requires everything to be in customer-owned VPC/DNS you'd need Private.
[05:45] Jamal: Can we get audit logs with raw prompts? Some legal folks want prompt redaction in logs.
[05:51] Alex: We have configurable retention and redaction policies. You can choose to store request metadata without the prompt, store a prompt hash, or keep full prompt in encrypted storage. We also integrate with SIEMs if you want push-based delivery.
[06:02] Sophie: I saw a note in your docs about KV cache — how does that surface in our architecture?
[06:08] Priya: The KV cache is an internal runtime optimization for transformer cache. From a user perspective, we expose a prefix cache option that lets you store repeated prefixes to reduce compute. If you're using a gateway, it can maintain a local prefix cache and avoid resubmitting the whole context for common prompts. Useful for assistant UIs with repeated system prompts.
[06:26] Mark: Let's do a quick example — our pipeline: user query -> retrieval from Pinecone -> LlamaIndex agent builds prompt -> Redwood generate -> post-process. Where does the gateway sit?
[06:36] Priya: Gateway sits between your application and Redwood endpoints. So after LlamaIndex prepares prompt, it hits the gateway which batches and enriches the request (adds auth, traces, prompt-hash), then gateway calls Redwood. Gateway can also call local embedding endpoint if you proxy that to Redwood embeddings.
[06:50] Jamal: Any sample topologies for high-throughput environments?
[06:53] Priya: Yes — we have three patterns: sidecar per service (low latency), centralized gateway cluster (easier ops, slight added latency), and edge adaptor (close to users). Each has tradeoffs for scaling and KV cache warmness. We'll share diagrams.
[07:06] Alex: Quick pause — does anyone have major constraint we haven't covered?
[07:10] Mark: Timeline: we want a pilot in 6 weeks, and production within 4 months if the pilot looks good. Budget is modest; we prefer predictable costs so Dedicated is interesting if committed throughput is high.
[07:23] Sophie: Also we have to pass security review — SOC2 and our internal pen test. We'll need a runbook for incidents and a topline on threat model.
[07:31] Alex: We'll send the security pack and SOC2 report. We can also do an architecture review session with your security folks.
[07:36] Jamal: On the SDK/adapter work — what's typical ramp time to swap in Redwood for LangChain LLMs?
[07:42] Priya: Usually it's a couple dev-days to wire the adapter into LangChain and validate streaming. If you want full tracing and cost attribution, add another day or two. We'll provide a sample repo that does most of that.
[07:55] Sophie: Are there open-source examples for LlamaIndex? We rely on that heavily for our vector retrieval glue.
[08:01] Priya: Yes, sample for LlamaIndex is included; it's a small VectorStoreClient that calls embeddings and stores metadata for provenance. I'll include it in the repo.
[08:10] Mark: Pricing — can you give high-level delta between Hosted and Dedicated? We won't get into contract, but ballpark numbers.
[08:18] Alex: Hosted is pay-as-you-go with per-token and embedding units, simpler for experimentation. Dedicated involves reserved GPU pools — you get lower effective per-token when you hit committed throughput. For RAG with heavy embeddings and steady inference, Dedicated usually saves money. We'll follow up with a side-by-side example using your traffic profile.
[08:36] Jamal: Regarding quotas: can we set per-customer caps inside our project? We need to throttle certain internal tenants.
[08:43] Priya: Yes, inside a single project you can issue multiple API keys with per-key quotas and different role permissions. Also RBAC supports route-level read/write controls.
[08:53] Sophie: Observability — can we export logs/traces to our Datadog?
[08:58] Alex: We have native integrations. We can push traces via OTLP to your Datadog endpoint or forward logs with a SIEM connector. You can also consume the Console API for programmatic exports.
[09:08] Mark: One more on the fallback behavior — if we pin a model version and you roll a patch, how are rollouts handled? We can't have sudden perf regressions at night.
[09:18] Priya: Rollouts honor pinning. We support canary policies per tenant. By default we route a small percentage to new variants and monitor quality / latency regressions. Console will surface evaluation metrics and if autoscale/fallback triggers.
[09:33] Jamal: Any limitations on function calling or structured outputs? We use JSON schema validation for downstream services.
[09:41] Priya: We support function calling / tool outputs and have a schema enforcement layer. If you pass a JSON schema we will attempt to produce structured JSON and will score responses for schema compliance in the Console.
[09:54] Sophie: Great — now for the nitty gritty: can you ship an example that demonstrates a gateway pooling 200 RPS of 100-token requests and shows P50/P99 with and without prefix cache?
[10:06] Priya: Yes — that's precisely the benchmark we usually run. We'll include a script to replay traffic, warm KV caches, and produce latency histograms.
[10:14] Alex: Ok, let's capture explicit next steps: I'll send the security docs and higher level pricing. Priya will produce the LangChain/LlamaIndex adapter repo and a benchmark script. Jamal will share a traffic export.
[10:25] Mark: Sounds good. Anything else?
[10:27] Sophie: One question on storage encryption — can embeddings at rest be encrypted with our customer-managed keys?
[10:33] Priya: For Dedicated and Private yes. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption with your KMS key in the supported region. We'll note the exact flows in the security doc.
[10:43] Jamal: Does Redwood support on-prem air-gapped deployment if we need it later?
[10:48] Alex: Yes that's the Private option — we have an on-prem package and a private control plane option. That said it's a longer lead time.
[10:55] Mark: Ok let's wrap. Thanks everyone.

Recap (auto):
- Redwood to send security pack, SOC2, and KMS integration docs (Alex)
- Priya to share LangChain and LlamaIndex adapter + benchmark scripts
- Jamal to provide traffic profile CSV and sequence length distribution
- Schedule benchmark session next week with infra team

[10:00 - end notes]: There were a few transcription quirks around product names — e.g., "KV cache" sometimes transcribed as "K V cash" and LlamaIndex as "Lama index". Some timestamps drifted during overlapping speech.

End of transcript.
